newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers wary of long Bosnia commitment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers wary of long Bosnia commitment.

text.p: Members of Congress reacted cautiously on Friday to President Bill Clinton's announcement he had agreed in principle to send about 8,500 U.S. troops to Bosnia as part of a new international peacekeeping mission.
Republicans charged that Clinton intentionally delayed announcing his decision to extend the mission until after the Nov. 5 elections, knowing it was likely to be unpopular with voters.

But despite his misgivings and his concern that Clinton had not leveled with voters, Indiana Republican Sen. Dan Coats, who opposed the initial Bosnia deployment, said he expected Congress to go along grudgingly with Clinton.
"There will be a lot of discussion but I think, at the end, the president having commited these troops, will receive support," Coats, a member of the Armed Services Committee, told reporters.
"At this point we have no choice but to remain part of a multinational force in order to attempt a resolution of at least some of the major problems" in the region, he added.
House International Relations Committee chairman Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican, said he was concerned that Clinton's decision would lead to open-ended military commitment.
"As I stated a year ago, setting an arbitrary departure date is no sustitute for an exit strategy and the tough decisions that must accompany one," he said in a statement.

Republican Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas said Clinton's announcement proved the administration's original claims about the scope and duration of the mission were unrealistic. She urged Clinton to call Congress, which has adjourned until January, into session to discuss his decision.

"I urge President Clinton to call the Congress into session so that he can explain in full detail how the commitments he is making today are any more solid than the commitments he made one year ago," she said in a statement.

When Clinton sent U.S. troops to Bosnia nearly one year ago, he promised Americans they would be out by the end of this year. In making his announcement on Friday, he said the peacekeeping mission in war-ravaged Bosnia had been successful but reconstruction of the government and economy had been slower than expected, making a follow-on force necessary.
Congressional Democrats appeared supportive of the president but were muted in their assessment of what the mission could accomplish in the long run.

"It seems clear that the president's decision is the right thing to do to prevent war from erupting again, a war which could spread elsewhere in Europe," Michigan Democratic Sen. Carl Levin said in a statement. "I am disappointed that it has not proved possible for the ... mission to bring an enduring peace to Bosnia," he said.

New Mexico Democratic Sen. Jeff Bingaman said the United States had a crucial interest in helping NATO ensure stability in Europe and called on lawmakers to support Clinton. "(The) policy that got us into Bosnia has (been) by and large bipartisan and the decision to remain there should be as well," he said.
